present attributive form of 가다, used to describe a following noun (e.g. “the road you’re going on”)

honorific form of 가다, used when talking about someone you respect (often before endings like -까요/-거예요).

definitions.native: should go, have to go, gotta go

definitions.note: Attributive form of 가엾다; used before a noun.

definitions.note: Polite (요-style) form; often used as an auxiliary meaning something is progressing/going in a certain way (e.g. “잘 돼 가요” = “it’s going well”).
polite present form (해요체) of 가다
present tense, polite (해요체) form of 가다

polite present form

definitions.native: bring it, get it and bring it

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can I pay by card here?

definitions.native: does it work?, is it okay?, is it possible?
definitions.note: Polite question form of 되다, used to ask if something is okay/allowed/possible or if something works.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay to take pictures here?

definitions.note: Adnominal (noun-modifying) form of the auxiliary 되다, used after a verb stem to mean something can be done or works.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 방법은 누구나 쉽게 따라 할 수 있는, 되는 방법이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method is a doable method that anyone can easily follow.

definitions.note: Attributive (modifier) form of 되다 used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 방법이 제일 잘 되는 방법이에요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This method is the one that works best.

definitions.note: Connector ending -는데 added to 되다; often sets background or contrast, like “but/though …”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It works now, but it won’t tomorrow.

definitions.note: From 되다 (“to become; to be okay/work”), used with -면 to mean “if/when …”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I have time, I'll call you.

definitions.note: Polite request form of 되다. Very commonly used in set phrases like “좋은 하루 되세요” (= have a nice day).
Honorific, polite ending used to confirm or gently ask for agreement (common in service situations).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: It’s okay if I pay with this card, right?

definitions.note: Conjugated form of 되다 used to connect to the next clause (like “becoming… / and then…”), or as “되어” in passive/causative-style expressions.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to Korea after becoming an adult.

definitions.native: see, it works; you know it works
definitions.note: Informal colloquial form of 되다 + -잖아, used to remind the listener of something obvious/known or to say “I told you so / see?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: See? If you do it like this, it works.

definitions.note: Contraction of "되지요"; often used to confirm or soften a statement (like “it works, right?” / “it should be okay, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, it works, right?

definitions.native: it’s okay, it works, you can
definitions.note: Polite ending used to soften the statement or seek agreement/confirmation (like “right?”). Often used with 되다 as an auxiliary meaning “be possible/okay.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, it’s okay, right?

definitions.note: Polite conversational ending (short for 되지요) often used to confirm or seek agreement, like “right?”
Auxiliary use of 되다 meaning something becomes possible/acceptable or works out. Often appears as part of patterns like “-면 되지” (“if you do that, it’s fine”) or “-도 되지” (“it’s okay even if…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do it like that, it works out / that’s fine.

definitions.note: Often used in questions or negatives like “되지?” (Is it okay?/Does it work?) or “안 되지” (It won’t work / It’s not allowed).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If I do it like this, is it okay?

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 되다, used before a noun to mean “that became” or “that is done/finished.”

definitions.native: that it works, that it will be (possible)
definitions.note: Used to quote or report a statement with -(ㄴ)다고 (e.g. “(someone) says that…” / “(someone) said that…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friend said that this method works.

definitions.note: future attributive form of 되다; used before a noun (e.g. ‘될 + N’ = ‘a N that will be/become’)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He is someone who will soon become a doctor.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it happen?
definitions.note: Used to wonder about a possibility or outcome; often expresses uncertainty.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?
definitions.note: Used to wonder or ask if something will be possible or acceptable.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will it work if I do it like this?

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be?
definitions.note: Used to wonder or ask if something will happen or be possible (되다 + -(으)ㄹ까).

definitions.native: will it be okay?, will it work?
definitions.note: Polite question used to check if something is acceptable/possible, or to ask for confirmation.

definitions.native: will it work?, will it be okay?
definitions.note: Polite question form used to ask if something is possible/okay (often like “would it be okay if…?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would it be okay if I sit here?

definitions.native: whether it will, if it will
definitions.note: The ending -(으)ㄹ지 expresses uncertainty or a question like “whether/if …”. Often used with 모르다 (“not know”) or 궁금하다 (“wonder”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't know if things will go well tomorrow.

definitions.native: is it possible, does it work
definitions.note: Formal polite question form of 되다, often used to ask if something is allowed/available ("Is it OK?").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can I pay by card here?

definitions.native: is it possible?, does it work?, is it done?
definitions.note: Formal polite question form of 되다; used to ask if something is okay/allowed/possible or if something works out.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay to take pictures here?

definitions.note: native Korean number used before a noun/counter (attributive form of 둘)
Connective form of 두다 used to link clauses (often meaning “after leaving/putting …”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I left the door open and went out.

definitions.note: Informal/casual form of 두렵다, often used before a following clause (e.g., “두려워서…” = “because I’m afraid…”).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저는 혼자 밤에 걷는 게 두려워요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m afraid to walk alone at night.

definitions.note: Often used with negation, e.g. 두지 마(세요) = “don’t put/leave (it).”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don't put your bag here.

definitions.note: 두통 means “headache.” 두통이 is used when “headache” is the subject (with the subject particle -이).
native Korean numeral (used before counters; e.g., 둘, 셋, 넷)
‘둘’ means “two (people/things)”; ‘-은’ marks it as the topic (“as for the two…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The two of them are friends.

definitions.note: Used when talking about two people/things as the subject (둘 + subject particle 이).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The two of them went to see a movie together.

definitions.note: Informal form of 두다, often used as a command ("Put it/Leave it").
Polite informal form; contraction of 두어요 from 두다.
Very rude slang/insulting command (strong profanity). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do that to me again, die.

definitions.note: Often used with verbs of movement to mean going to the back or moving backward.
Used to indicate a position/time that comes after another person/thing/event; commonly used with a noun + 뒤에.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The bag is behind the chair.

definitions.native: behind, in back of; after, later
definitions.note: 뒤에 is 뒤 (“back/behind”) + the location/time particle 에 (“at/in/on”), so it can mean both a place (“behind”) and a time (“after”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There is a park behind the school.

definitions.note: Informal past form. Often used when looking through something thoroughly.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I rummaged through my wallet for a while.

definitions.note: Very informal and can sound harsh; often used as slang (e.g., jokingly ‘I’m dead’).
Conjugated form (from 들다) often used to mean “when/after (someone) entered …” in narrative style.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When I entered the house, the lights were off.

definitions.note: Commonly refers to a device/tool like a screwdriver, or a driver (software) for hardware.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I installed the printer driver on this computer.

definitions.note: Polite form; humble/honorific way to say ‘give’ when giving to someone (especially someone older or higher status).
Humble/polite form used when offering to do something for the listener (from 드리다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall I carry your bag for you?

definitions.note: Honorific/polite; used to offer to give something to the listener (or someone respected).

definitions.native: shall I give it to you?, would you like me to give it to you?
definitions.note: Polite offer/question form of 드리다 (“to give (to someone respected)”). Often used when offering help or handing something to someone.

definitions.native: please eat, please have (some), please take (it)
definitions.note: Polite imperative/honorific form used when asking someone (often older or a customer) to eat or take something.
polite past honorific form (used when talking about someone you respect)

definitions.native: will eat, would you like to eat?
definitions.note: Polite, honorific form (from 먹다 → 드시다) with -겠- often used to express intention or a polite offer/question.
honorific form (for someone respected); often used to modify a noun (e.g., 드실 음식 “food to eat”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The food you will eat is ready.

definitions.note: Polite question using the honorific form (드시다). Often used when offering food to someone (e.g., a customer or an older person).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Would you like to eat dinner?

definitions.note: Used after nouns/verbs in choices like “A든 B든” to mean “whether A or B / whichever.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Coffee or tea is fine (either one is okay).

definitions.note: Connects to the next verb/clause, meaning “and then/and (while) …” (verb stem + -고).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I listen to music and study.

definitions.note: Used with the ending -지 (often followed by 않다/못하다/마(요)), e.g. 듣지 마(요) = “don’t listen.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please don’t listen to music right now.

definitions.note: Added after a noun or pronoun to show “more than one,” often used with people (e.g., 친구들 “friends”). It’s often optional when the plural is already clear from context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The students are in the classroom.

definitions.note: This form is the verb stem of 들다, used before endings (for example, 들+고 → 들고).
From 들다 (“to hold, lift, carry”); -고 links to the next verb or clause (“and/while”), so 들고 often means “holding/carrying (and then…)”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went home carrying a bag.

definitions.note: From 들리다 (“to be heard; to be audible”). Often used to say something is audible or that you can hear something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You can hear the music well from here.

definitions.note: Polite present form of 들리다; often used to mean “I can hear it” or “It sounds/comes through.”
Casual/questioning ending -나; often sounds rhetorical or like talking to oneself. From 들리다 (“to be heard”).
casual/informal form (can be used as a command like “listen!” or as casual speech like “(I) hear/listen.”)
Informal present form; also used as a casual command meaning “come in.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I come in? Come in.

definitions.note: Often used as an informal command meaning “Go in/Go inside.”
Often used as an informal command meaning “go in/come in.”

definitions.native: even if (someone/something) goes in, even if (someone/something) enters
definitions.note: From 들어가다 + -아/어도 (“even if / even though”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it okay if I go in now?

definitions.note: Conditional form of 들어가다, used to mean “if/when (someone) goes in/enters.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you go inside, please take off your shoes.

definitions.native: must go in, have to enter
definitions.note: From 들어가다 (“to go in/enter”) + -아/어야 (“must/should”). Often used with 해/돼 (e.g., 들어가야 해/돼).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Right now, you have to go into the building.

definitions.note: polite present tense (요 form); can also be used like “go (ahead) inside” depending on context
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m going into the house now.

definitions.note: Polite request/suggestion (often translated as “please listen”).
informal command (casual speech); often used like “listen (to me)” / “hear me out.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Listen to me for a second.

definitions.note: Polite suggestion/request form; often used like “Listen to me.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please listen to what I’m saying.

definitions.note: Polite request/command form, often used when inviting someone inside a room or building.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The door is open. Please come in.

definitions.note: Informal/plain style; used to tell someone to come inside or to say someone is coming in.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I opened the door, so come in.

definitions.note: polite informal present tense; often used to invite someone to enter
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The door is open. Come in.

definitions.note: Polite present tense of 듣다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m listening to music right now.

definitions.native: will you listen (to me)?, will you hear me out?
definitions.note: Informal request form (often used when asking someone to listen or to accept a request).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will you listen to me for a moment?

definitions.note: Informal past-tense question; often used when asking if someone heard something (can sound slightly blunt).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

definitions.note: Very informal, blunt/rough question (past tense), often used with close friends or in confrontational speech.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

definitions.note: Used to express uncertainty or an indirect question about having heard something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m curious whether you heard the news.

definitions.native: did you hear?, did you listen?
definitions.note: Informal past-tense question (to a friend/younger person).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Did you hear what I said?

definitions.note: informal speech (to friends, someone younger, etc.)
informal speech (to friends, someone younger, etc.)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I lifted the bag with one hand.

definitions.note: Past tense, polite style.
Past tense, polite style.
Past tense with the ending -죠, often used in conversation to confirm or assume agreement (like “you heard it, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You heard the news yesterday, right?

definitions.note: Past tense with the ending -죠, often used in conversation to confirm or assume agreement.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I picked up that box, right.

definitions.note: Past tense of "to hear" with the ending -지, often used to check/confirm something (like “..., right?”) or remind someone (“you know ...”).
Honorific, past tense, with a tag question meaning “..., right?”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You heard the announcement just now, right?

definitions.note: Past modifier form of 듣다, used before a noun (e.g., 'the story (I) heard').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The story I heard was really interesting.

definitions.note: Future/intentional modifier form of 듣다 used before a noun (e.g., 들을 음악 “music to listen to”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: There is a lot of music to listen to.

definitions.native: if (someone) gets caught, if (something) is found out
definitions.note: From 들키다: to be caught / to be found out (often about a secret).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If they find out it's a lie, you're in big trouble.

definitions.note: An insult; rude and offensive.
A loanword commonly used in cafés and restaurants.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I eat dessert after a meal.

definitions.note: Informal/polite style ending (-해). Can describe temperature, weather, or a warm/comfortable feeling.
Informal command (casual speech) meaning “follow (me)” or “go after (someone/something).”
Informal casual command form (used with friends, kids, etc.).
Polite ending (해요체); often used as a request like “Please follow/come with me.”
Often used to mean doing something not together or keeping things not mixed.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I sat separately from my friend.

definitions.native: things like that, anything like that
definitions.note: Contraction of 따위(‘such a thing’) + 는. Often used to dismiss or belittle something (like ‘that kind of thing’ / ‘anything like that’).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Don’t worry about things like that.

definitions.note: Often used to mean something fits or matches perfectly, or a number/time is exact.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 이 신발이 내 발에 딱 맞아.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These shoes fit my feet exactly.

definitions.note: Commonly used before a noun in casual speech (e.g., 딴 사람 = “another person”).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My daughter is six years old.

definitions.native: as for (my/your/his/her/the) daughter, daughter + topic marker
definitions.note: 딸은 = 딸 (daughter) + 은 (topic marker). It means “as for the daughter / the daughter (as the topic)” and the exact person (my/your/etc.) comes from context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: As for the daughter, she goes to school.

definitions.note: Polite form of the copula ‘이에요’ used after a noun ending in a consonant (딸 + 이에요).

definitions.native: on the ground, in the ground
definitions.note: Particle -에 marks a location ("at/on/in").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The ball fell to the ground.

definitions.note: Often used to mean “when” in the pattern “-(으)ㄹ 때” (e.g., 갈 때 = when (someone) goes).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I lived in Korea when I was young.

definitions.note: "때" means "time/occasion"; "때가" is "때" + the subject marker 가.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Right now is not the time to eat lunch.

definitions.native: until (the time when), up to (the time when)
definitions.note: Used after a time expression or a clause (often with -(으)ㄹ 때) to mean “until.”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll wait until you arrive home.

definitions.note: Informal speech level (해체).
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 동생이 자꾸 놀려서 한 번 때려 줬어.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My younger sibling kept teasing me, so I hit them once.

definitions.note: Used after a noun (or a clause with -기/-(으)ㅁ) to give a reason/cause.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I stayed at home because of the rain.

definitions.note: Casual/informal speech level (plain style with -야). Used to explain a reason.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The reason I'm late is because of traffic.

definitions.note: Contraction of "때문이지요"; "-지요" adds a gentle/confirming tone (like “you know / right?”).
Used to wonder/guess the cause or reason; often follows a clause (e.g., ~해서/~인) and has a questioning tone.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 피곤해서 그런 때문인가 자꾸 실수를 해요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is it because I’m tired? I keep making mistakes.

definitions.note: Contraction of 때는 (“as for when…, at the time when…”). Commonly used with clauses like ~할 땐 (“when (someone) does…”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: When I'm busy, I can't answer the phone.

definitions.note: Often used in the command 눈 떠! (“Open your eyes!”) in informal speech.
Casual/plain style (informal).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The boat is floating on the water.

definitions.note: Informal/casual form used in speech; can be used as a command (“Leave!”) depending on context.
Polite (해요체). Depending on context, it can also sound like a suggestion: “let’s leave.”
Used with a negative ending (e.g., 떠나지 마, 떠나지 않았어).
This is the verb stem + -(으)ㄹ, used to mean “will/going to leave” or “to leave” (as in “the time/day to leave”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m going to leave tomorrow morning.

definitions.note: past tense of 떠나다
informal past tense of 떠나다
Casual/informal present tense ending (-아/어).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: An apple falls from the tree.

definitions.note: Past tense of 떨어지다. Used for something falling physically or a level/amount going down (e.g., temperature, grades).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The phone fell to the floor.

definitions.note: Describes something that has fallen/dropped (past modifier form of 떨어지다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I picked up the apple that fell on the floor.

definitions.note: Polite past tense. Commonly used for things like the sun, the moon, or bread rising.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The sun has already come up.

definitions.note: Slang and insulting/vulgar; used to call someone ‘crazy’ in a rude way.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That person seems like a weirdo.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 똑같다; used before a noun.
Informal/plain style form of 똑똑하다 (often used in casual speech).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My younger sibling is really smart.

definitions.note: Often means doing something correctly (not crooked, not incorrectly), as well as literally straight.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please sit up straight in the chair.

definitions.note: Slang; literally means “poop car,” used to describe a very bad/old car.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 저 똥차는 또 시동이 안 걸려.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That crappy car won’t start again.

definitions.note: present attributive form of 뛰다; used before a noun (e.g., “a running person”)
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I can see a person running.

definitions.note: Casual/informal present form of 뛰다; also used in commands like “Run!” depending on context.
Polite present tense (해요체) of 뛰다.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I run every morning in the park.

definitions.note: Informal/polite casual ending (-어), commonly used in speech.
Used with 않다/못하다 (e.g. 띄지 않다) to mean “not stand out.”
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 옷은 너무 화려해서 멀리서도 띄지 않아?
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That outfit is so flashy—doesn’t it stand out even from far away?

definitions.note: Attached to a noun/phrase to suggest a minimal or second-best choice.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Please give me at least some water.

definitions.note: Attached to a noun/phrase to emphasize that something is surprising or unexpected ("even ...").
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 아이도 아니라도 그렇게 말하면 안 돼요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Even if you’re not a kid, you shouldn’t talk like that.
I listen to the radio in the morning.

definitions.note: A small device used to make a flame (e.g., for cigarettes or candles).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I drank water with lemon in it.

definitions.note: Particle used after nouns. Means direction (to/toward), means/method (by/with), or role/status (as). Often pairs with “(으)로” depending on the final consonant of the noun.
object particle used after a noun that ends in a vowel (the consonant-ending form is 을).

Object particle used after a noun that ends in a vowel (variant of 을/를).

definitions.note: Often used in Korean addresses as part of a place name (e.g., ○○리).
A type of Italian pasta (long, flat noodles).
informal; often used in spoken Korean as a sharp command (like “Stop!”), sometimes heard in regional speech
Used after a verb stem as an imperative to tell someone not to do something (e.g. 하지 마 = don't do it).

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: A witch appears in that story.

definitions.note: Common in casual speech; can sound rude or sexist, so it’s safer to use 아내 in polite situations.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My friend said he got scolded by his wife.

definitions.note: Common informal/nonstandard spelling of "많이" (often seen in casual writing).
An old-fashioned/historical term used to address or refer to the wife of a nobleman or the female head of a household; commonly heard in historical dramas.
A negative command from the auxiliary 말다, used after a verb with -지 (e.g., 가지 마라 = “don’t go”).

informal command (to a friend/child): “drink!”

definitions.note: Usually refers to magic tricks/illusion (like a magician does).

definitions.note: Often refers to a face mask (for health/safety), but can also mean other kinds of masks.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I wear a mask when I go outside.

definitions.note: Often used in set phrases like ‘마스터하다’ (to master) or for roles/titles (e.g., game master).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to master this skill.

definitions.note: From 마시다 (“to drink”) + -고 (“and/then”), used to connect to the next verb/clause.
Attributive (noun-modifying) form of 마시다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Who is the person drinking water?

definitions.note: Polite question form of 마시다 (to drink). Often used to offer or suggest drinking something.

definitions.note: Used as the ending -지 마요 to tell someone not to do something (polite).

Object form (마음+을), used when 마음 is the object of a verb.

definitions.note: With the subject particle -이 attached to 마음 (“heart/mind”).
Used before a noun (like a determiner): “the last/final (one)” or “the last/final + noun.”
Often used to introduce the final point in a list or sequence (like “lastly,” “finally”).

definitions.note: Future/intentional modifier form of 만나다, used before a noun (e.g., “the person I will meet”).

definitions.note: informal command form ("touch/feel it")

modifier form of 말하다 used before a noun (e.g., ‘something to say’)

casual; often used to ask someone to speak or explain (like “go on, tell me”)

definitions.note: Polite way to ask someone (often with respect) to give you something; from 주다 with honorific -시- and the request ending -(으)ㄹ래요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Could you give me this, please?

definitions.native: please (do it for me), please give (me)
definitions.note: Polite formal request form of the auxiliary 주다, used after another verb to mean “please do (that action) for me.”
used for the main character in a story, movie, drama, etc.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The main character of this movie is a young girl.

definitions.note: Honorific/polite form of 주인; used when respectfully addressing the owner/master (e.g., a pet’s owner or in historical/servant-like contexts).
“주제가” is “주제” (topic) with the subject particle “-가”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: What's the topic of today's meeting?

definitions.note: Casual ending using -지; often sounds like a soft request or a mildly complaining tone (similar to saying ‘come on, give it to me’).
Often used to mean “to the point of dying / extremely,” or as “죽게 만들다” = “to kill.”
Connective form of 죽다 meaning “die and…/die, and then…”, linking to what comes next in the sentence.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그는 전쟁에서 죽고 많은 사람들이 슬퍼했어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He died in the war, and many people were sad.

definitions.note: Nominalized form of 죽다 (“to die”), often used to talk about the act of dying or death in general.
Attributive form of 죽다 used to modify a noun (e.g., “a dying person/animal”).
Present tense, plain style (often used for statements, narration, or casual speech).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Flowers die if they don’t have water.

definitions.note: Informal/casual present form (also used to tell someone/something to die, depending on context).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: The flower is dying because it doesn’t have water.

definitions.note: A very harsh/insulting command; can be used in curses.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Die right now, away from me!

definitions.native: like crazy, as hard as possible
definitions.note: Often used before a verb to mean doing something extremely hard (e.g. 죽어라 공부하다).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I studied like crazy because of the exam.

definitions.note: Often used with a following verb (e.g., 죽어야 해요/돼요) to mean that dying is necessary/inevitable.
Past tense of 죽다 (“to die”). Often used as “(someone) died,” or colloquially to mean “I’m dead/exhausted.”
Used to quote or report speech/thought with -다고 after the past tense of 죽다 (“to die”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: They said on the news that the actor died.

definitions.note: casual/informal past form (used with friends, kids, etc.)
polite past tense (informal polite style)
Informal/casual command form (like “Kill (it/him/her)!”). Often used jokingly or as slang in phrases like “나 죽여” (“I’m dying!” / “This is killing me!”).
An imperative command; very direct/harsh. Can also be used in fiction as an order (e.g., “Kill him/her/them”).

definitions.native: I'll kill (you), I'm going to kill (you)
definitions.note: Informal speech; often used as a strong threat or as an exaggerated/joking way to say you're very angry.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I swear, I'm going to kill you.

definitions.note: This form combines 죽이다 + -어 버리다, often adding the feeling of doing it completely or with strong emotion. It can be used literally or as an exaggerated threat in casual speech.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do that again, I’ll seriously kill you.

definitions.note: Past tense with the casual question ending -나; often used in informal speech, sometimes as a self-directed question (“did I…?”).
Past tense of 죽이다 (“to kill”).
Common slang meaning something was done extremely well (not literally “killed”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: You absolutely crushed it on stage today!

definitions.note: Past tense of 죽이다 (“to kill”) + -다고, used to report a statement (“said that …”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He said that he killed a bug.

definitions.note: A quoted statement form of 죽이다 in the past: 죽였다는 = “(someone) said that (they/he/she) killed …” or “the claim that (someone) killed …”
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He said that he killed the bug.

definitions.note: casual/polite past tense (as in speech between friends)
Polite past tense of 죽이다 (“to kill”). It can also be used casually to mean “That was awesome/amazing,” depending on context.
Polite past tense with a nuance like “(I/you/he) did, right?” or recalling/confirming something.
Common informal/slang use of 죽이다 meaning something was “killer” (really good).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Yesterday’s performance was really amazing, right?

definitions.note: From 죽다 (“to die”) + -(으)면 (“if/when”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you die, the insurance payout comes out.

definitions.note: Attributive form of 죽다, used before a noun (e.g., “dead person”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: A dead fish is floating in the water.

definitions.note: Attributive (noun-modifying) form of 죽다, used before a noun.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He has an illness that will kill him.

definitions.note: Future attributive form of 죽다, used before a noun (e.g. 죽을 병 “a fatal illness”).
object-marked form of 죽음 (with 을), used when it is the direct object in a sentence
Connects to the next verb or clause, like “and then…”.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I killed the mosquito and closed the window.

definitions.note: Used to express purpose: “in order to kill.”

definitions.native: to try to kill, in order to kill
definitions.note: Used with -(으)려고 to express intention or purpose.
definitions.example_sentence_target_language: 그 남자는 나를 죽이려고 칼을 들었어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That man picked up a knife to try to kill me.

definitions.note: Often used as a casual ending like “-지” to add emphasis, as in “죽이지!” = “It’s killer!” / “Awesome!” (not literal).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: That movie is seriously awesome, right?

definitions.note: Past attributive form of 죽이다, used to modify a noun (e.g., “the person (someone) killed”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: He buried the animal he killed.

definitions.note: Often also used casually to mean something is amazing or very intense (e.g., 맛이 죽인다 = “it tastes incredible”).
Often used before a noun to mean “killer/amazing” (slang), but literally it means “to kill” as a modifier.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I don't have the strength to kill.

definitions.note: A casual question ending (-을까) meaning “should I…?”/“shall I…?”. Often used playfully or as a threat depending on context.

definitions.note: This is the verb 죽다 with the ending -지, commonly used before 않다 (not) or 말다 (don’t), e.g. 죽지 마(요) = “don’t die.”
Often used with 하다 (준비하다/준비를 하다) to mean “to prepare.”
Casual/informal question ending (-나), often used by a speaker addressing someone younger or close.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Is everyone ready? Let’s head out now.

definitions.note: Informal casual speech. Often means “(I’m) ready” or “Are you ready?” depending on context.
Polite speech style. Often used to mean “I’m ready,” but can also mean something is prepared/ready depending on context.
Direct object form of 준비 with the particle 를.
Informal/polite spoken form of 준비하다 (as in 준비해요).

definitions.native: will do for (someone), will give (as a favor)
definitions.note: Used as the auxiliary form of 주다 after another verb to mean doing that action for someone (a favor/service). Often appears inside longer forms like -줄게요, -줄까요, -줄 수 있어요.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’ll carry your bag for you.

definitions.native: will give, to give (as a modifier)
definitions.note: Form of 주다 used before a noun (e.g. 줄 사람 “the person who will give”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: This is a gift I’ll give you.
People are standing in a line.
I tied the box with a rope.

definitions.note: Often used before 것 (e.g., 줄 거야) or before a noun to mean “(someone) will give.”

definitions.note: Informal. Used after a verb to promise/intend to do something for someone (e.g., 도와줄게 = I’ll help you).
Used to ask oneself or someone for a suggestion/decision; often means “Should I give it to you?” depending on context.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Should I give this to you?

definitions.native: should I give (it), shall I give (it)
definitions.note: Often used to offer something or ask for a suggestion; from 주다 (“to give”) + -ㄹ까 (“shall I?/should I?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Should I give you coffee? / Want some coffee?

definitions.native: shall I give (you)...?, would you like me to give (you)...?
definitions.note: Polite question/offer form of 주다 (“to give”), used to ask if you should give something or do something for someone.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Shall I give you some water?

definitions.note: Used to make a casual, friendly request. Often follows a verb stem (e.g., 해 줄래? "will you do it for me?") or 주다 "to give".
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Will you give me this, please?

definitions.native: will you (do it)?, can you (do it) for me?
definitions.note: Polite request form (often used after a verb stem), asking someone to do something for you.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Can you help me with this?

definitions.note: An informal command form (like “Reduce it/Shorten it”).

definitions.note: object particle -을 attached to 줄 (“line/row”).

definitions.note: Informal speech: 줄 + 이야 (“is”). Used to say something is a 줄.
Used after a noun to mean something is currently happening (e.g., 회의 중 = during a meeting / in a meeting).

definitions.note: Often used as a bound noun in patterns like “N 중(에/에서)” meaning “among N / out of N.”

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Out of three people, one person is a student.

definitions.native: in the middle of, during (in progress)
definitions.note: Often used as a bound noun meaning something is currently happening (e.g., “회의 중” = “in a meeting”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m in a meeting right now.

definitions.note: This form includes the object particle 를, so it often marks “Chinese” as the direct object of a verb (e.g., learn, study, speak).
Informal/casual speech (ending -야), used after a noun.
used to mean “among” a group or “out of” a set (often with superlatives or choices)

definitions.note: Often used before 않다 (e.g., 중요하지 않아요). In casual speech it can also end a sentence by itself.

definitions.note: Informal polite style ending; a common spoken form of 중요하다.
a military rank (commissioned officer)
used in math/statistics to mean the middle value

definitions.note: Informal ending. Used after a verb in the form -는 중이야 to mean you are in the middle of doing something.
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I’m doing my homework right now.

definitions.note: Often used in formal contexts for stopping or suspending an activity (e.g., work, service, operations).

definitions.note: Informal/casual request form of the auxiliary 주다 used after a verb (like -아/어 줘) to mean “please do it for me/someone.”

definitions.note: informal command/request form of 주다; often used like “give me …” depending on context

definitions.native: give it to me, hand it to me
definitions.note: Casual command/request. Often used when asking someone to hand you something; can also be used when asking to show something (like “let me see”).

definitions.note: Polite form of 주다 (“to give”). Often used after another verb to mean “do (it) for me” (e.g., 도와줘요 = “please help me”).
Polite present tense of 주다 (“to give”). Often used as a request, like “please give me … / please do … for me.”
Casual/polite (해체) past form of 주다 used as an auxiliary to show doing something for someone (often implying a favor).

definitions.note: Attributive form of 즐겁다 used before a noun.

definitions.note: Often used for legal or investigative contexts, but also in everyday situations.

Casual/informal present form of 증오하다; it’s very strong (closer to “despise”).

definitions.note: Used after a clause to make an indirect/embedded question.

지금 (“now”) + topic particle 은; often used to mean “as for now / right now” depending on context.

definitions.native: it’s now, now is the time

used before a noun to refer to the time period before now (e.g., 지난주 = last week)

지하철 + 로 (“by/through”), indicating means or route.

Object-marked form of 진실 with the particle 을.

Used to emphasize that you really mean something; often with apologies, thanks, or feelings.

Polite form often used as a request/command (e.g., to a customer, stranger, or someone you should be respectful to).

Polite form, often used as an instruction/request to someone.

Often used in casual speech for emphasis, like “really?” or “seriously?” depending on context.

definitions.note: Used to quote a command/order (하다 + -라고). Often followed by verbs like 하다/말하다/시키다 (e.g., 하라고 했어요 = 'told (me) to do it').
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: My mom told me to do my homework.

definitions.note: Used when repeating or emphasizing an instruction/command; often has the nuance of “I’m telling you to do it.”

definitions.native: (someone) said/told (someone) to do, that (someone) should do
definitions.note: From 하다 + -라는; used to quote a command/request and modify a following noun (e.g., 하라는 말 ‘words telling (someone) to do’).

definitions.native: I told you to do it (so...), I’m telling you to do it
definitions.note: Spoken, casual form of "하라고 하니까". Used to emphasize a command or to complain that someone isn’t doing what you told them to do.

definitions.note: used to express purpose, often followed by 가다/오다 (go/come)

definitions.note: Used after a verb stem to express purpose or intention (e.g., 하려고 = “(in order) to do / intending to do”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the park to exercise.

definitions.note: From 하다 + -려고; used to express intention or purpose ("(in order) to do").
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I went to the park to exercise.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to describe someone/something that is about to do something or has the intention to do it.

definitions.note: -면 conditional form of 하다 (“to do”); often used to mean “if you do (it)” or “when you do (it)”.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: If you do your homework, you can play games.

definitions.note: polite (해요체) form of 하다; often used in requests or instructions.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Write your name here, and also sign.

honorific attributive form of 하다; used to describe a noun (e.g., “the person who does…”)

definitions.note: honorific form of 하다, used when talking about someone you want to show respect to (often used before a noun, like 하실 일 “the thing you will do”).

definitions.note: An interjection expressing a sigh (e.g., tiredness, frustration, relief).

definitions.note: Casual spoken form of 하지 않잖아. Used to remind someone or insist/emphasize something (often like “I told you / you know I do”).

definitions.note: From 하다 (“to do”). Commonly used with 요 for polite speech; often adds a soft suggestion/assumption like “(we) do it, right?” depending on context.

informal spoken form of 하지 마 (“don’t do [it]”)

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: I want to go, but I don't have time.

short form of 하나; commonly used before a noun in counting (native Korean numbers)
Past adnominal (modifier) form of 하다; used to describe a noun (e.g. ‘the thing (someone) did’).

Plain (informal) present tense form of 하다; often used in writing, narration, or informal speech.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Hanja (Chinese characters) help you understand Korean vocabulary.

definitions.note: Used before a noun to mean “to do” / “that will be done” (e.g., 할 일 = “things to do”).

definitions.note: This is the modifying form of 하다, used before a noun to mean “to do” / “that (someone) will do.”

Polite question ending used to make a suggestion or ask for someone’s opinion/decision (often like “Shall we…?” or “Should I…?”).

definitions.note: informal/casual; used to show intention or to ask someone’s choice (often with 1st/2nd person)

definitions.note: Polite ending that shows intention or willingness ("I’ll do it / I want to do it"). It can also be used to ask someone if they want to do something, depending on context.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Grandpa takes a walk in the park.

definitions.note: Often used to mean doing something without enough thought or respect (e.g., speaking or touching something).

I always drink coffee in the morning.

definitions.note: Casual/informal. Used to suggest trying something or to wonder out loud whether to do it.

definitions.example_sentence_native_language: Work is so hard these days.

definitions.native: it was hard, it was tough, right?
definitions.note: Casual/polite-sounding ending: past tense of 힘들다 (“to be hard/tough”) + -지, often used to confirm or empathize (“..., right?” / “..., wasn’t it?”).
Sentence-ending form used to say something is hard/tiring or to check/confirm it (like “It’s hard, right?”).
definitions.example_sentence_native_language: These days there's a lot of work, so it's hard.
